questions.stem: What is a boundary case in unit testing?

options.text: A common scenario the function is expected to handle.
An edge case that tests the limits of the function's input space.
A situation where the function should handle invalid input gracefully.
A scenario that is unlikely to occur in real-world usage.

questions.explanation: Boundary cases are designed to test the limits of the input space, ensuring the function behaves correctly at the edges of its expected input range.

questions.stem: Why is it important to include error cases in a test suite?

To verify the function handles invalid inputs gracefully.
To confirm the function's performance under load.
To reduce the number of tests needed.

questions.explanation: Error cases test how a function handles invalid inputs, ensuring it fails gracefully without crashing or producing incorrect results.

questions.stem: Explain why testing only the happy path in a program can lead to false confidence. Provide at least two reasons.
markingGuide: Happy path tests only cover scenarios where everything works as expected.
They fail to account for edge cases and unexpected inputs.
Without testing edge cases, potential bugs may go unnoticed.
Real-world usage often includes unexpected inputs, leading to failures.
questions.explanation: Testing only the happy path may miss edge cases and unexpected inputs, leading to undetected bugs. Real-world scenarios often include such cases, so a program may fail in practice despite passing happy path tests.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of unit testing?

options.text: To improve the performance of the code.
To verify the correctness of small, isolated parts of the code.
To ensure the code is well-documented.
To reduce the size of the codebase.

questions.explanation: The primary goal of unit testing is to ensure that individual components of the code function correctly, providing a foundation for reliable and maintainable software.
